en: The Sūtra on the Hells Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha...
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If there are three things in a person, they are the characteristics by which a foolish and unworthy person is judged.
What are these three things?"

When a foolish person harbors evil thoughts, speaks evil words, and performs evil deeds, they incur calamity in this very life, suffering through their body, suffering through their thoughts, and suffering through their anxieties.
What constitutes sorrow and suffering?
When a foolish person associates with a wise one, the wise person speaks of the path, saying that because the fool has committed evil deeds, he shall enter hell after death.
The fool then thinks to himself regarding what the wise person has said:
"Thinking, 'Now that I have committed evil, upon death I shall enter hell,' this is the suffering of anxiety.
What is the suffering of reflection?"

Fools see those who steal wealth and, with cruel malice, employ shackles and fetters to bind them; they cut off their hands and feet, whip them with bamboo whips and leather thongs, and feed them to tigers; or they place them in iron cauldrons and set them ablaze, or hack them limb from limb with axes and mallets, or pin them to the ground for elephants to trample, or place them atop cauldrons or in steamer-vessels to boil them, or seize their four limbs alive and tear them apart.
The foolish man thinks to himself:
"The wicked person committed an outrageous act, leading the official to subject me to such torture.
If the official were to know that I have also done evil, he would surely seize me in the same way."
This is what is meant by mindfulness of suffering. What is physical suffering?

A foolish person, from morning until night, finds no peace in their sleep or waking; their mind constantly dwells on evil, their mouth constantly speaks evil, and their body constantly performs evil. After these evils have been committed, when they fall ill, they see themselves as one among those in the cauldrons of fire in hell. They see people being burned and see people being boiled; the transgressions and evils they have committed gradually come to torment them, just as after midday, the shadow gradually lengthens.
As that person enters slightly further, the wicked beings within the *niraya* immediately think to themselves:

"While I was in the world, I delighted in killing, delighted in stealing, delighted in violating the wives of others, delighted in deceiving people, delighted in double-tongued speech, delighted in harsh speech, delighted in false speech, delighted in envy, and delighted in stinginess and greed; I did not believe in the Buddha, I did not believe in the Sūtras, I did not believe that the causes and conditions one creates bring about calamity or blessing, and I did not believe in rebirth in future lives—this has caused me to die and enter the *niraya*."
"This is what constitutes physical suffering.

The Buddha said, "Suppose an evil person were to have eyes like mine; if they were to see the places where the wicked go to undergo calamities, transgressions, and tortures, that evil person would immediately be terrified, their heart would wither and break, and they would die vomiting boiling blood."
The Buddha said:
"If you wish to know that which is most unbearable in its diligent suffering, it is found only in the niraya hells.
As for the nirayas, their extreme suffering cannot be fully described."
The bhikṣus knelt with their right knees on the ground and said,
"We wish to hear an analogy for the diligent suffering of the niraya hells.
The Buddha said:
"It is like a high official who captures a rebel and brings him before the king, saying:
'This man has committed treason and harbors evil thoughts against the state.
The king commands the official to pierce the man with spears until he has a hundred wounds."
The next day he asked him,
"What kind of person is this?
and he replied:
"Shangsheng," the king said,
"pierce him with another hundred wounds."
The next day, he asked him,
"What kind of person was he?
He replied:
"He is still alive.
The king said,
"Pierce him with another hundred wounds."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If a person were to be struck with three hundred wounds, would there be any spot remaining intact even as large as a jujube leaf?
The bhikṣus replied:
"There is not a single intact spot," the Buddha said to the bhikṣus.
"This man has been afflicted with three hundred sores; is he not suffering from excruciating pain?"
The bhikṣus said, "If a person receives a single wound, their entire body suffers pain; how much more so when they receive three hundred wounds!
The Buddha took a small stone, placed it in his hand, and showed it to the bhikṣus.
"Is this stone large,
or is Mount Tai large?
The bhikṣus replied:
“The stone in the Buddha’s hand is small; how can it be compared to a mountain?
Even if one wished to compare it to a mountain, it would still fall short of the mountain’s size by billions upon billions of times.
The Buddha said:

"The pain in the hells is hundreds of billions of times greater than the pain of a spear wound; even so, it does not equal the pain of hell. The small stone in his hand is like three hundred spear wounds, while the mountain is like the pain within hell."
A person of deluded mind who commits evil in thought, evil in speech, and evil in deed will, after death, fall into the *niraya* hells.

Within the *niraya*, there are beast-like spirits who drag the person forward, hooking their upper gums with a hook and then hooking their jaw; the mouth is forced wide open, and molten copper is poured into the person's mouth. The lips, tongue, intestines, and stomach are all scorched and rotted away; as the copper flows down, the agonizing pain is unbearable.

Because that person, throughout their life in the world, sought wealth and profit and consumed food and drink wastefully, molten copper is poured upon them; such is the diligent suffering in the niraya.

In the hells, demons seize people and hook their upper and lower jaws with hooks, pulling them wide open. They then take a red-hot iron pestle and thrust it into the person's throat; the lips, tongue, intestines, and stomach are all scorched and rotted away. The agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. Such is the intense suffering of the hells.

The ghosts within the *niraya* hell further seize people and lead them up an iron mountain; they set fire to the mountain until it glows a vivid red, and the victims run up and down it. The agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions have not yet been expiated, they do not die; such is the diligent suffering of the *niraya*.

The ghosts within the *niraya* hell further seize people, using glowing red axes to sever their hands, sever their feet, and sever their hundred joints, cutting them apart limb by limb; the agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die—the diligent suffering of the *niraya* is thus.

The ghosts within the *niraya* hell further seize people and hack their bodies with iron axes until the flesh and bones of their entire bodies are completely consumed. The poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions have not been exhausted, they do not die; such is the diligent suffering of the *niraya*.

In the niraya there is a bird with a beak like iron, which pecks at people’s heads and devours their brains; the agony is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die—such is the intense suffering of the niraya.

Within the niraya there are also herds of wild asses that together seize human corpses to devour and gnaw upon them; the poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions have not yet been exhausted, they do not die—such is the diligent suffering of the niraya.

The ghosts within the *niraya* hell further seize people and flay them with knives from their two thighs and intestines up to their two sides. They force them to pull iron chariots, using the flesh from their sides as a cloak. They compel them to drag the iron chariots across blazing fires; the agonizing pain is unbearable, yet they do not die because their transgressions have not yet been expiated. Such is the diligent suffering of the *niraya*.

The ghosts in the niraya hell further seize the two legs of a person and hurl them upside down into a cauldron; as the broth boils and surges, those at the bottom are cooked and those at the top are also cooked; boiling up and down repeatedly, there is none who is not cooked.

It is like boiling beans: those at the top and bottom are cooked equally; whether covered or exposed, they are cooked alike. So it is with those in the *niraya* hells: wherever they are, they are cooked, for there is no distinction of east, west, above, or below.
This is the result of how that person, while living in the world, allowed their mind, speech, and body to run wild. Such is the diligent suffering of the *niraya* hells.

The ghosts within the *niraya* hell seize people again and lay them upon the red ground to be treated with the five poisons. They drive glowing iron nails through their left palms, then drive glowing iron nails through their right palms; they drive glowing iron nails through their right feet, then drive glowing iron nails through their left feet; finally, they drive glowing iron nails through their hearts, piercing all the way down to the earth. The agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. Such is the diligent suffering of the *niraya*.

"In the niraya, the ghosts drag people by the arm into the city of niraya. The city of niraya is perfectly square, with gates on all four sides; the city walls are solid on all four sides, and each gate has guarding ghosts."

The walls and the ground of that city are all made of iron, and the city is covered with iron so that nothing may leak through; the ground is glowing a brilliant crimson. It extends four thousand li in circumference. The flames from the eastern wall reach the western wall, the flames from the western wall reach the eastern wall, the flames from the southern wall reach the northern wall, and the flames from the northern wall reach the southern wall. The flames above descend to the ground, and the flames from the ground rise to the heights.

All evil persons who commit these ten deeds fall into this state: those who kill living beings, those who steal, those who violate the wives of others, those who deceive people, those who engage in double-tongued speech, those who speak harsh words, those who utter falsehoods, those who are jealous, and those who are stingy and greedy; as well as those who do not believe in the Buddha, do not believe in the sutras, and do not believe that the causes they create result in calamity or fortune.
In this manner, such people fill the hells.
Within the hells, they suffer extreme agony for tens of millions of years before they suddenly see the eastern gate open and all run toward it.

Those whose feet touch the ground are immediately scorched; when they lift their feet, the flesh grows back as it was before. Those who are destined to escape pass through and depart, while for those not yet destined to escape, the gate closes once more.
When that person saw others who had managed to escape, yet found himself unable to do so, he looked intently around and fell prostrate on the ground.
The gate-keeping ghost said, "Hey, you wicked dead man! You have come to this gate; what do you seek?"
He said, "I am hungry and thirsty.

The ghost then took the hook and hooked his upper and lower jaws, pulling them wide open; he then poured molten copper into the man's mouth, which scorched and rotted his lips, tongue, intestines, and stomach, before the copper passed through and went out below.

Throughout that person's life in the world, they sought wealth and profit without recourse to principle; because of the evil and rebellious acts they committed, they now undergo such calamity, enduring such diligent suffering in the hells.

"Furthermore, there is a hell like a worldly furnace of glowing embers, several thousand li in length and breadth. All the people flee from their cities and rush into this charcoal-fire hell; they are scorched, roasted, and cooked until they are withered, finding no rest. The poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. Such is the diligent suffering within this hell."
"Next, they enter again the Cold Ice Hell (Hima-naraka), which is several thousand li in length and breadth.

When people enter within it, they are all frozen and shiver with cold; their bodies are shattered and split apart. The poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions have not been expiated, they do not die; such is the diligent suffering of this hell."
"Furthermore, they enter the Kukkula (Boiling Excrement) hell, which extends for thousands of li all around. The excrement is hot and boiling, emitting a foul stench;

one rushes toward it and enters. Once inside, one is cooked there by oneself; the poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because the transgressions have not been exhausted, one cannot die. Such is the diligent suffering of the hell."
"Furthermore, they enter the Pus-and-Blood Hell, which extends for thousands of li in every direction; its foul stench is beyond description, and the pus and blood all boil.

Having fallen into it, their bodies are completely cooked and rotted away until they are ruined; they are devoured by crows and birds, and the poisonous pain is unbearable. Because their transgressions have not yet been expiated, they cannot die; such is the diligent suffering of the hell."

Next, they enter the Razor Mountain, which extends for thousands of li in circumference. People fleeing from the Pus-and-Death Hell run toward the mountain; when they attempt to climb it, the blades upon the mountain cut their feet.
Just as they try to brace themselves, they have their hands cut off;
just as they try to move forward, their bellies are sliced open.
Just as he wished to lie down, they cut through his back;
just as he wished to sit, they cut through his hips;
just as he wished to lean, they cut through his ribs.
The poisonous pain is unbearable; yet because their transgressions have not been expiated, they do not die. Such is the diligent suffering in the hells.
Next, they enter the Sword-Tree Hell, where the branches of the trees are all like swords.

When a person enters therein, swords pierce their chest, their ribs, their back, their hands, their feet, and their bodies; piercing through from front to back, the agonizing pain is unbearable. Yet because their transgressions have not yet been expiated, they do not die; such is the diligent suffering of the *niraya* hells.
"Next, they enter the Iron Bamboo Reed Forest, which is several thousand li in length and breadth; its leaves are all like sharp blades.

When people enter therein, the wind blows through the reeds, causing them to vibrate; the leaves pierce their flesh and sever their bones, leaving no part of their bodies intact. The agony is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die—the diligent suffering in this hell is such as this."

"Next, there is the entrance into the Salt Water Plow Hell, which is thousands of li in length and breadth. The salt water is like brine, boiling and surging with heat. Within the water there are birds with beaks like iron plows; they peck at human flesh and gnaw at human bones. When the people can no longer endure this pain, they cross over the water and flee."
The guardian of the hell spoke, saying:
"You wicked dead man, what do you seek?
The person replied:
"I am suffering from hunger and thirst.

The ghost then uses a hook to pull apart his upper and lower gums until his mouth gapes wide open; he then pours molten copper into the person's mouth. His lips are scorched, his tongue is scorched, and his throat is scorched; all five internal organs within his belly are completely consumed by the fire. The copper then flows straight through him. The person can no longer endure it and returns once more to the boiling brine.

The suffering was as before and could not be endured; he returned again to enter the iron reeds and rushes, where the suffering was as before and could not be endured; he returned again to enter among the sword-trees, where the suffering was as before and could not be endured; he returned again to enter the Razor Mountain, where the suffering was as before and could not be endured; he returned again to enter the mire of pus and blood hell, where the suffering was as before and could not be endured; he returned again to enter the boiling excrement hell, where the suffering was as before and could not be endured; he returned again to enter the charcoal fire hell, where the suffering was as before and could not be endured; he returned again to enter the iron city hell, where the suffering was unbearable.
The suffering at the eastern gate is likewise; the suffering at the southern gate is likewise; the suffering at the western gate is likewise; the suffering at the northern gate is likewise.
Such is the diligent suffering of the niraya.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The sufferings of the hells are beyond counting; I have merely described them to you in brief and in their coarsest form.
The Buddha said:
"When a person commits evil, they are reborn among the animals, where they feed on grass, licking with their tongues and chewing with their teeth.
What is meant by 'licking with the tongue and chewing with the teeth'?"
There are many such [beings] as oxen, horses, mules, donkeys, elephants, wild asses, and camels.

During their lives in the world, these people harbored evil thoughts in their minds, spoke evil words with their mouths, and performed evil deeds with their bodies; after death, they transmigrate and are reborn as these animals, undergoing such diligent suffering.
The Buddha said:
“There are birds and beasts that are born in darkness, grow up in darkness, and die in darkness.
What is meant by being born in darkness?
Snakes, rats, raccoon dogs, otters, insects, ants—beings of such various kinds are numerous.

When such people dwelt in the world during their lifetime, they harbored evil thoughts in their minds, spoke evil words with their mouths, and committed evil deeds with their bodies; after death, they transmigrate through successive births to become these birds and beasts, enduring such diligent suffering.
The Buddha said:
"There are scaly creatures that are born in water, grow in water, and die in water.
What is meant by 'born in water'?"
The various species such as crocodiles, dragons, fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, and alligators are as numerous as this.

When such people were alive in the world, they harbored evil thoughts in their minds, spoke evil words with their mouths, and committed evil deeds with their bodies; after death, they undergo successive transformations to become these scaly creatures, suffering such toil and hardship.
The Buddha said:
"There are worms that are born in stench, die in stench, and grow in stench.
What is meant by being born in stench?"
There are many such species as worms in marshes, worms by ditches, and worms in latrines.

Having lived in the world throughout their lives with evil thoughts in mind, evil speech in mouth, and evil deeds in body, they have become these kinds of insects and worms after death, undergoing such diligent suffering.
The Buddha said:
"There are insects and animals that feed primarily on impurities; when a person changes their clothes, they smell the odor from afar, run toward it, and say, 'I have found food.'"
What constitutes those whose impurity consists primarily of food?
There are many such species as dogs, pigs, flies, dung beetles, and other things belonging to the foul and filthy class.

During their lifetimes in the world, these beings harbored evil thoughts, spoke evil words, and committed evil deeds with their bodies; after death, they have transmigrated through various states to become such insects and animals, enduring such diligent suffering.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The insects and animals are numerous; I have merely given you a rough account for your sake.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"When a person commits evil and is reborn among the *preta* (hungry ghosts), they constantly eat boiling excrement and urine.
Why do they constantly eat boiling excrement and urine?

Because while that person was living in the world, their mind conceived evil, their speech uttered evil, and their body performed evil; being stingy and greedy for food and drink, they are thus reborn among the *preta*."
Furthermore, the preta take pus and blood as their food. Because such beings, while living in the world, committed evil deeds and were addicted to delicacies, they now eat pus and blood.
Within the realm of the pretas, there are black dogs and white dogs that primarily feed on the flesh and limbs of the pretas.
Within the Pretas there are crows that feed primarily on their brains.

Some have not seen water for ten years; some have not obtained water for a hundred years. Others may see flowing water from afar, perfectly clear, and wish to go toward it to drink; yet when they approach, the water has vanished into emptiness.
Or at times, the water transforms into molten copper.
In some places, brackish water boils like a cauldron;
just as they wish to step forward and drink, the ghosts strike them.
Such is the diligent suffering within the realm of the *peta* (hungry ghosts).
The Buddha said:
"The pretas are numerous; I have merely given you a rough explanation.
The Buddha said:

"It is difficult for a person in the three evil realms to escape from them. It is like this: suppose there were water extending eighty-four thousand li all around, and within it was a blind turtle; on the surface of the water was a floating log with a single hole. If the turtle were to emerge with its head out of the water once every hundred years, would it ever happen to place its head within the hole of the log?"
The bhikṣus said:
"Even after hundreds of thousands of millions of years, we fear we may not enter it. Why is this? Because—"

Sometimes the wood is in the east and the tortoise is in the west; sometimes the wood is in the west and the tortoise emerges from the east; sometimes the wood is in the south and the tortoise emerges from the north; sometimes the wood is in the north and the tortoise emerges from the south; and sometimes the tortoise has just poked out its head when the wood, driven by the wind, lands upon dry land.
"A turtle that emerges from the water only once every hundred years still has the chance to put its head through a hole;
for a person to be born as a human while dwelling in the three evil realms is even more difficult than for that turtle."

Why is this? Because those in the three evil realms have no sense of knowledge or discernment, nor do they possess any moral law; they do not distinguish between good and evil, nor do they recognize their parents, nor do they understand the practice of giving. Instead, they prey upon one another, the strong forcibly devouring the weak.

People such as these have never been free from the wounds of slaughter, flaying, pus, and blood; they pass from suffering into suffering and from darkness into darkness—such is the experience of the wicked.
The Buddha said:

"Suppose there is a person who has lost much of his property at first, until he has lost even his wife, children, fields, and house; reduced to being emaciated and barefoot with nothing left remaining, he still continues to carry the burden of what is owed."
"The master of wealth severely rebukes him, fumigating him with smoke and roasting him with fire.
The Buddha said:

"For one who is thus oppressed, what he loses is still relatively slight; yet initially he loses much, eventually losing even his wife, children, fields, and houses. Furthermore, owing the remainder of the debt, he is subjected to such fumigation and roasting by others. Thus, he remains poor for a lifetime, with only a few remaining years to count."

If a person harbors evil thoughts in the mind, speaks evil words with the mouth, and performs evil deeds with the body, after death they will fall into the three evil realms; this poverty exceeds even that.

Having spent incalculable eons within the three evil realms, even if one attains liberation from them and is reborn among humans, one will become a craftsman, or the son of a poor beggar living in the wilderness, or one who must provide for oneself through manual labor, unable to satisfy oneself with fine clothing.
Although one may be born as a son within such a family, one might at times be lame, deaf, or blind, unable to associate with others.

Or, if born into a family of slaughterers—whether they sell oxen and sheep, or butcher fish, deer, chickens, and dogs—one emerges from an evil path only to become the son of such a household; committing further evil, one shall, after death, return once more to the evil paths.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"With my divine eye, I behold all people in the world—their births and deaths, their beauty and ugliness, the noble and the lowly, and those who, upon death, attain a good destination or a bad destination."

If a person in this world commits evil through their bodily actions, evil through their speech, and evil through their thoughts, and constantly delights in slaughtering living beings to offer as sacrifices to spirits and deities, they shall enter the hells after death.
"If one constantly performs good with the body, constantly speaks good with the mouth, and constantly dwells on good with the mind, upon death one will be reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha said:
"A person is like bubbles arising in rainwater; as the rain falls from above, one bubble breaks and another forms."

In this world of human life, those who are born and those who die appear and vanish like bubbles; with his divine eye, the Buddha beholds all people throughout the world—those in the heavens and those entering the hells, the poor and the wealthy, the noble and the lowly—and observes the good and evil deeds performed by each person.
The Buddha said:
"I know them all. It is like this:

suppose it were a dark night, and at both sides of a city gate, great torches were lit; there were tens of millions of people going out and coming in, and from the darkness, everyone could see those entering and exiting within the light of the fires."

The Buddha, with his divine eye, beholds those ascending to the heavens and those entering the hells, just as a person looking from the darkness sees others entering and exiting a fire, or as a person atop a high tower sees all the houses below—some tens of thousands in number—as they look down from above.
The Buddha said:
"I see those among the people of the world who, upon death, ascend to heaven or enter niraya (hell), just as a person from atop a high tower looks down upon various households."
The Buddha said:
“It is like a person traveling by boat through clear water, seeing all the fish and stones within the water.
When the Buddha uses his divine eye to observe the people of the world—those born in the heavens and those entering the hells—it is as if that person were looking into clear water.”

In the world there is a bright moon pearl; if one threads it with a five-colored cord, when people look at the pearl, they all see the five colors distinctly, and they know the cord and the pearl, perceiving them as being threaded through one another.
The Buddha perceives the cycle of birth and death, the good and evil, and the transformations of all beings in the world as clearly as a person beholding a pearl.
The Buddha said:

"I see those in the world who are unfilial toward their parents, who do not serve śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, who do not respect their elders, who have no sense of duty, and who neither fear nor are awed by this life or the life to come—such persons, upon death, immediately enter hell."
Upon meeting King Lavana, one immediately abandons evil and turns toward good.
The wardens of Niraya are named Pāṅga; Pāṅga leads the person from the human realm to the presence of King Lavana, and the wardens of Niraya address him, saying:

"When this man was in the world, he was unfilial toward his parents, failed to serve śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, did not respect his elders, took no delight in giving, feared neither this world nor the next, and had no dread for the prohibitions and precepts. We pray that Your Majesty will adjudicate this man’s transgressions."
The king immediately summoned the man before him and addressed him, saying:

"When you were a human being in this world, did you not think of your parents who nurtured you? When you were pushed onto straw mats and fed with milk while living in dampness until you grew large, how could you have been unfilial toward your parents?"
The man immediately replied:
"I am indeed foolish and arrogant.
The king said:
"Regarding those who dwell in transgression, it is not the fault of their parents, nor of the heavens, nor of emperors or kings, nor of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
Whatever one has done with one's own body, one must receive that for oneself."
This was the first question of King Sāgara. [He asked:
"If one does not see people in the world when they are afflicted by severe illness, becoming exceedingly emaciated and weak, their hands and feet rendered useless?"
The man said,
"I truly saw it. The king said:
"Why do you not reform yourself and practice goodness?
The person replied,
"I am truly foolish and arrogant."
The King said:
"If it is what one has done with one's own body, one must receive its consequences oneself.
This is not the fault of parents, nor of heaven, nor of a sovereign, nor of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"If one acts with the body, one shall surely receive the fruit thereof.
This was the second question of King Sāgara. [He continued:

"Have you not seen the men and women of this world when they grow old—their eyes seeing nothing, their ears hearing nothing, walking with a staff, their black hair turning white, no longer like that of their youth?"
The man replied,
"I truly saw an old man walking with a staff.
[The Buddha asked,] "At that time, why did you not change yourself to do good?"
The man said,
"I am indeed foolish and arrogant.
The king said:
"This is not the fault of your parents, nor of the heavens, nor of the sovereign, nor of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
It is what you have done with your own body; you shall surely receive its fruit yourself."
This was the third question of King Sāgara. [He asked:

"If, during the course of time in this world, one does not see a man or a woman die, but [sees them] for one day, two days, up to seven days, their bodies rotting and their physical forms decaying, being devoured by worms and ants, and becoming loathsome to all people?"
"If you see this, why do you not reform yourself to become good?
The man replied, "I truly see it; I am foolish and arrogant."
"If one practices such deeds, why not rectify one's conduct, rectify one's speech, and rectify one's mind?
This is not the fault of parents, nor of heaven, nor of emperors and kings, nor of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
"If one acts with the body, one shall surely receive the consequences oneself.
This was the fourth question of King Śālibhadra.

"Furthermore, when you were among men in this world, did you ever see officials seize robbers or murderers, bind them hand and foot, and send them to prison to be flogged and interrogated; or see them led out onto the road and beaten to death, or dragged alive and torn apart? Did you ever see such things?"
The man said, "I truly saw it. [The Buddha asked:
"Why did you not reform yourself and do good?"
"When you were a human being, why did you not rectify your body, rectify your speech, and rectify your mind?
The person replied,
"I was truly foolish and arrogant."
"If it is produced by one's own body, one must receive its consequences oneself.
This is not the fault of parents, nor of heaven, nor of emperors or kings, nor of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"Whatever one does with the body, one shall receive that for oneself.
This was the fifth question and response of King Yama.
When the questioning and responding were finished, the attendants of Niraya led him away and brought him before an iron city; this was the first hell, named Avīci Niraya.

The city has four gates and is four thousand li in circumference. In its center is a great cauldron forty li in length and breadth, and also forty li in depth. The hell-wardens pierce people with spears and cast them into the cauldron to boil them.
In this way, there were fires within countless cities; when people saw them from afar, they were all filled with sorrow, fear, and trembling.

Thus, tens of millions of people entered, as the hell-wardens pursued them and cast them inside. Day and night they could not enter or exit; though they ran toward the four gates seeking an egress, all the gates were closed and they could not get out.
People remain within it for many tens of millions of years; the fire does not extinguish, nor do the people die.

After a long time, they see the eastern gate open of its own accord, and everyone runs toward it wishing to escape. Just as they reach the middle of the gate, the gate closes again, and those who wish to exit begin to fight and quarrel with one another at the gate, vying to get out.

After a long time, they again saw from afar the southern gate open; they all ran toward it, but the gate closed once more, and everyone began to fight and struggle with one another at the gate, desiring to get out.

After a long time, they again saw from afar the northern city gate open; they all ran toward it, but the gate closed once more, and everyone again began to fight and struggle with one another at the gate, desiring to get out.
After a long time, he again saw from afar the western gate open; everyone ran toward it, but the gate closed once more.
After a long time, all four gates opened again; everyone ran toward them and was able to escape entirely, believing themselves to have attained liberation.
"Furthermore, they enter the second Kūṭana hell; as their feet touch the ground while running, they are instantly scorched, yet when they lift their feet, the flesh grows back as it was before.

Some run east, some west, some south, and some north; the ground all around them is hot and scorched. Only after many tens of millions of years does it come to an end, at which point they imagine they have finally escaped."
"Furthermore, they enter the third hell, Mīḍhadeha. Within it there are insects; these insects are named Khārodaka, with iron-like muzzles and black heads."

When these insects see a person, they all fly toward them to peck at them, devouring their flesh, marrow, and bones until nothing remains; only after many tens of millions of years does this finally come to an end, at which point the being thinks it has escaped.

"Furthermore, they enter the fourth hell, Paṅkavatī. Within it are stones as sharp as knives; people all run toward their peaks, while some run down, all seeking escape, yet not knowing how to go about it. Their feet are all sliced and flayed, for the stones of the ground are all like sharp knives. Thus they endure for many tens of millions of years before finally reaching the end, at which point they believe they have escaped."

"Furthermore, they enter the fifth hell, Āvapāta. Within it there is a hot wind; the wind is so intensely hot that it exceeds the glowing coals of the world. When the wind strikes their bodies, it scorches them. Those who wish to avoid it always encounter the hot wind; though they try to flee, they cannot escape."
That person seeks death but cannot die; they seek life but cannot live. After thus passing many tens of millions of years, they finally emerge, believing themselves to have attained liberation.
"Furthermore, they enter the sixth hell, A-yu-can-bo-li-huan (Āpāṇaka), where there are many trees; all these trees consist of thorns, and between the trees dwell demons."
When a person enters therein, fire issues from the ghost’s head and fire also issues from its mouth; the entire body is covered with sixteen spikes.

Seeing the person approaching from afar, the ghost erupts in a great rage and comes forward to devour the person’s flesh, piercing the person’s body with all sixteen spikes and tearing it apart to eat it.
Everyone desires to escape, yet as they run, they constantly encounter these ghosts. After doing so for many tens of millions of years, they finally reach the end and believe they have escaped.

They enter again into the seventh hell, *Saptama-tapana-niraya*. Within it there is a worm named *Dun*; when a person enters it, this worm flies in through their mouth and devours their body. All the people run to the utmost limit, seeking release, but the worms devour them without ceasing. They run in all directions but cannot escape; after doing so for many tens of millions of years, they finally reach the end and believe they have escaped.

"Furthermore, they enter the eighth hell, Tāpanīya. Within it there is a flowing river; all people fall into the water, and along the banks are thorny brambles. This water is hotter than boiling water in the world; it seethes and surges, so that all who are in it are cooked and rotted."
They ran toward the shore, but on the bank there were demons holding spears who pierced people with their hands and thrust them back inside so they could not escape.
Once the people entered, they were all carried downstream by the current; at the lower reaches there were more demons, who intercepted and hooked them, asking:
"From where have you all come?"
"If it is for this reason,
why is it so? The person said,
"I do not know from where I have come, nor do I know how I shall go."
"I am merely suffering from hunger and thirst, and wish only to pursue food.
The ghost said,
"I shall give you food."
He immediately took molten copper and poured it into his mouth, yet it burned him through to the marrow; thus he sought death but could not die, and sought life but could not live.
Because that man committed evil while he was a human being in the world, he seeks liberation but cannot attain it.

"All the beings in the hells were able to emerge again, each thinking they had attained liberation; yet upon returning, they entered once more into the seventh hell. There, the spirits of the seventh hell came forward to greet them and asked:
'Having already departed, why have you returned? "
The inhabitants of all the hells all said, "We suffer only from hunger and thirst.

They immediately entered the sixth hell, and from the sixth they entered the fifth; from the fifth they entered the fourth; from the fourth they entered the third; from the third they entered the second; and from the second they entered the first, the Avīci Mahānaraka, seeking release. From afar they beheld an iron city, and with great joy they cried out loudly, all together proclaiming, "Ten thousand years! (Jaya!)
When the King of Salt heard this, he immediately asked the hell-warden:
"What kind of sound is that?
The hell-warden then replied:
"This cry is from those who have gone to the hells previously.
King Yama said:

"These were all those who were unfilial toward their parents, who did not fear heaven, who did not fear the sovereign, who did not revere their ancestors, who did not serve śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and who did not fear the prohibitive precepts."
The King of Salt saw them again and said to them:

"If you are indeed not the King of Salt, and now that you have all been liberated and departed, should you become children of men, you must be filial and obedient; you must serve your elders well; you must stand in awe of Heaven; you must stand in awe of the sovereign; you must attend upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; and you must rectify your mind, rectify your speech, and rectify your body."
While living in this world, one's transgressions may be small and light, yet the punishments of the hells are vast and heavy;
if one serves śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, one shall thereafter attain liberation from all evil realms, and the gates to places of diligent suffering shall be closed forever.
When the dialogue was concluded, all those within the hells were able to emerge outside the city walls, where they all died that very night.

Those who had died while previously being human—though they had committed much evil, they still possessed some small merit—and who returned from the hells, all became upright again according to the Way. Having emerged from the hells, each with a rectified mind and upright conduct, they would no longer return to enter the hells;
nor would the hells call for them. Because of their evil deeds, they had undergone the cruel and poisonous suffering within the hells, yet they may now reflect upon themselves and practice goodness.
When the Buddha had thus taught this instruction, the bhikṣus were all filled with joy.
This concludes the Niraya Sūtra spoken by the Buddha.
